source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray, Ashley (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: LLMs in Hierarchical Legal Reasoning
finding: Three-task test of distinguishing a precedent from a current case, built on the CATO factor hierarchy. A symbolic solver gives exact ground truth. Models are perfect on surface differences and weak when they must combine hierarchy steps.
numbers: Task 1 (find distinctions): 100% for all 6 models. Task 2 (argumentative roles in hierarchy): 64.82% (gemini-flash) to 92.09% (gpt-5). Task 3 (all significant distinctions): 11.46% (gemini-flash) to 33.99% (qwen3-thinking); most under 25%. n=253 per task.
quote: All models achieve perfect performance (100% accuracy) on Task 1
limits: Synthetic cases in the CATO trade-secret factor domain, not real opinions. Six models only; thinking-token counts are provider-reported.
agent_relevance: Similar in law is not surface overlap. Make the agent compute likeness stepwise (distinction, role, significance) and check each step in code, not in one pass.

source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray, Ashley (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: LLMs in Hierarchical Legal Reasoning
finding: Reasoning mode matters a lot for hierarchical likeness judgments.
numbers: qwen3 thinking 78.66% vs qwen3 non-thinking 30.04% on Task 2. On Task 3 the non-thinking model scores 0.00%.
limits: One model family for the comparison. Gains mostly vanish on the integrative task.
agent_relevance: A reasoning pass is needed for analogy-by-role, but it does not fix integration. Supports splitting the integration step into program-counted sub-steps.

source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray, Ashley (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: LLMs in Hierarchical Legal Reasoning
finding: More thinking is not better. Models spend more tokens on wrong answers than right ones.
numbers: gpt-5 Task 2: 4,456 tokens when wrong vs 3,081 when right (+45%). gpt-5 tokens rise 487 (T1) to 3,189 (T2) to 7,025 (T3), 14.4x. qwen3-thinking uses 9,596 tokens on T2 (3.0x gpt-5) for lower accuracy (78.66% vs 92.09%).
limits: Correlation across items; difficulty may drive both length and error.
agent_relevance: Token length is a usable trouble signal: a long trace on an analogy step should trigger a decomposed retry or abstention, not more thinking. Fits the rule of not trusting written reasoning.

source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray, Ashley (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: LLMs in Hierarchical Legal Reasoning
finding: Trace analysis: models miss that a factor strongly supports an issue through a concern, then mark the wrong factor as significant. Long traces loop without converging.
numbers: Qualitative traces from qwen3-thinking and gpt-oss-120b on one Task 3 item.
limits: Single-instance trace analysis.
agent_relevance: Likeness depends on which differences matter for the rule's purpose, not how many differ. A program-held factor hierarchy would prevent this error.

source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray, Ashley (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: LLMs in Hierarchical Legal Reasoning
finding: Authors conclude current reasoning post-training (maths and logic) does not give hierarchical legal skill and suggest new training data.
numbers: Models: gemini-flash, gemini-pro, gpt-oss-120b, qwen3 thinking and non-thinking, gpt-5. Temperature 0.3 for Gemini and Qwen.
limits: Opinion in the discussion; no test of alternative training.
agent_relevance: Our route is a scaffold, not training; the same evidence says the scaffold must supply the hierarchy.

source: Zhang, Gray, Savelka, Ashley (2025) Measuring Faithfulness and Abstention: Automated Pipeline for LLM 3-ply Case-Based Legal Arguments
finding: Eight LLMs write 3-ply arguments (cite precedent, distinguish it, cite a second, rebut) from factor sets. They rarely invent factors when an argument exists, but often leave out available ones and fail to refuse when no shared factors exist.
numbers: Hallucination accuracy Test 1: GPT-4o 99.64%, Llama-3-8B 92.39%, DeepSeek-R1-Distill 91.38%. Factor-use recall T1: GPT-4o over 85%; GPT-4o-mini about 42-50%; others 50-70%.
limits: Synthetic factor-represented cases; factors extracted by a GPT-4.1 judge (spot checked); 30 abstain items per model.
agent_relevance: Faithful to inputs yet incomplete. List all shared and unshared features in code, then let the model only phrase the argument.

source: Zhang, Gray, Savelka, Ashley (2025) Measuring Faithfulness and Abstention
finding: Abstention test: when the precedents share no factor with the case, models told to decline mostly write an argument anyway.
numbers: Abstention ratio: GPT-4o 86.67%, Qwen-QWQ-32B 56.67%, Llama-4-Maverick 50.00%, DeepSeek-R1-Distill 23.33%, Llama-3-70B 3.33%, Llama-3-8B, Llama-4-Scout, GPT-4o-mini 0.00%. Test 3 hallucination accuracy fell to 84.91-99.16%.
limits: One prompt design; instruction-only abstention.
agent_relevance: No-analogy-exists must be a code-checked state: if the shared-factor set is empty, the program blocks argument generation. Model self-restraint fails.

source: Zhang, Savelka, Ashley (2025) Do LLMs Truly Understand When a Precedent Is Overruled?
finding: 236 US Supreme Court overruling pairs (1789-2025), median opinion 17,607 words. Models struggle to name the overruled case from the overruling opinion.
numbers: Task 1 open ID: Gemini-Pro 73.31% (173/236), GPT-5 71.19% (168/236). Task 2 verify true pair: GPT-5 75.42%, Gemini-Pro 42.37% (131 answered unknown). GPT-5 said False in 55 cases.
limits: Only explicit overruling; GPT-4o as judge; temperature 0.1; one time point.
agent_relevance: Precedent status (still good law) cannot be left to model memory or one read. Use a citator lookup and a verification step. Models often give only one of several overruled cases.

source: Zhang, Savelka, Ashley (2025) Do LLMs Truly Understand When a Precedent Is Overruled?
finding: Models pass a reversed-direction control (did the older case overrule the newer?) but fail the real task, so success there is shallow chronology. They also invent temporally impossible links in open answers.
numbers: Task 3 reversed control: GPT-5 100%, Gemini-Pro 100%, Qwen3 97.46%. Era sensitivity: older eras much worse; in one interval Qwen3 1.54%, Flash-Lite 0.00%, best 24.62%.
limits: Era effect is confounded with text length and archaic language.
agent_relevance: Add cheap code-side sanity checks (dates, court hierarchy) on every precedent claim. Treat old-case reading as high risk.

source: Fan et al. (2025) Legal Rule Induction: Generalizable Principle Discovery from Analogous Judicial Precedents
finding: Task: from 5-10 similar cases, induce a rule (condition, behaviour, consequence). Benchmark LRI-GOLD has 216 case sets (1,620 Chinese cases), expert annotated. A rule counts only if it applies to over half the set (Levi-style generalisation from a case cluster).
numbers: Direct prompting micro-F1: Claude-3.7-Sonnet 66.67%, Gemini-2.5-Flash 60.51%, GPT-4o 55.50%.
limits: Chinese civil-law data linked to statutes, so easier than common law. Gold rules come from annotators.
agent_relevance: This is the Levi step, case to case via a rule. Induce a rule from analogues, then verify it against each case: a usable operator.

source: Fan et al. (2025) Legal Rule Induction
finding: Scaffolds change results. The SILVER pipeline (induce, verify each rule against cases, iterate) beats direct, CoT and long-CoT prompting. CoT raises precision but cuts recall. Fine-tuned small models beat larger prompted ones.
numbers: GPT-4o with CoT: Mic-Pre 71.81 to 80.95 but explicit-rule recall 55.56 to 41.63. Llama-3.2-3B Mic-F1 19.21 to 70.96 after LoRA on LRI-AUTO; Ministral-8B +LoRA 73.18 vs Gemini-2.5-Flash direct 60.51.
limits: SILVER costs the most tokens. Small-model gains are in-domain on auto-built data.
agent_relevance: Induce-then-verify-per-case is an evidence-backed loop shape. Test it with a token budget.

source: Fan et al. (2025) Legal Rule Induction
finding: Set size sensitivity: more input cases lead to lower precision and higher recall (overgeneralisation). Claude-3.7-Sonnet and DeepSeek-V3 stay stable; GPT-4o-mini and Llama-4-Maverick degrade more.
numbers: Direction of effect from Figure 5; set sizes 5 to 10 cases.
limits: No per-size numbers read from the text.
agent_relevance: Use small, similar clusters when abstracting a rule; cap set size and verify.

source: Fan et al. (2025) Legal Rule Induction
finding: Dataset building used a cross-case applicability count: explicit rules kept only if they apply to 100% of cases in the set; implicit rules kept above a threshold. An LLM did the applicability check.
numbers: Quality audit of the checks reported about 93-100% yes on checklist items (Table 6).
limits: LLM-checked-by-LLM, plus a human sample check.
agent_relevance: A cross-case applicability count is a program-countable check that suits the guardrail against self-grading.

source: Demir & Canbaz (2026) Validate Your Authority: Multi-Label Precedent Treatment Classification
finding: Classifying how a later case treats a precedent (overruled, criticised, distinguished) on 239 expert-annotated citations. Accuracy mostly tracks class frequency.
numbers: Gemini 2.5 Flash 79.1% on the high-level schema; GPT-5-mini 67.7% on the fine-grained schema. Largest class (156 items) F1 0.864; NEUTRAL (10 items) F1 0.400; 7 of 15 fine labels F1 0.000. Over 19% of items have more than one valid label.
limits: Small set, one jurisdiction, zero/3-shot only, label subjectivity sets a ceiling.
agent_relevance: Fine labels like distinguished vs questioned are not learnable zero-shot. Use coarse categories.

source: Demir & Canbaz (2026) Validate Your Authority
finding: Proposes an Average Severity Error metric because confusing INVALIDATED with NEUTRAL is worse than confusing CRITICIZED with QUESTIONED.
numbers: Per-label F1: INVALIDATED 0.764, CRITICIZED OR QUESTIONED 0.651, CONFLICT NOTED 0.480. Few-shot used 3 random examples excluded from the test set.
limits: Metric proposed, not validated elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Weight errors by cost when the agent checks whether a precedent still holds.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) A Reasoning-Focused Legal Retrieval Benchmark
finding: Finding the relevant law often needs analogical or multi-hop reasoning with little word overlap, which standard retrievers miss.
numbers: Recall@10 BM25 vs E5-large-v2: Bar Exam QA 5.03 vs 7.00; Housing Statute QA 18.3-40.8 vs 24.4-50.6 (lower/upper bound); NQ 40.4 vs 68.7. Housing corpus about 1-2M documents.
limits: Statutes and bar-exam questions, multiple choice. I could not map the COLIEE and CLERC columns with certainty.
agent_relevance: Word-level similarity search is a poor proxy for legal likeness. Retrieval for the agent needs a step that states the abstract rule first.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) A Reasoning-Focused Legal Retrieval Benchmark
finding: Query expansion with a structured legal-reasoning rollout (GPT-3.5) beats plain CoT expansion and paraphrase. Gains are largest where lexical overlap is lowest.
numbers: CoT over baseline Recall@10: Bar Exam QA +7.37 (E5-base), NQ +1.59, HotpotQA -2.79. Structured vs CoT: +3.09 (Bar, E5-large), +8.97 (Housing, E5-large).
limits: Better retrieval did not always help the answer: gold passage raised Llama 3 8B only about 20%; the reasoning pseudo-passage confused GPT-4o-mini on Bar Exam QA. On Housing, retrieved passage gave +23.53 points over none.
agent_relevance: Operator: restate the question as the governing abstract rule before searching for analogues. Retrieval gain is capped by the reader.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) A Reasoning-Focused Legal Retrieval Benchmark
finding: Authors argue that deciding which law is relevant is a separate legal reasoning skill, so retrieval and reasoning should be tested together.
numbers: Bar Exam QA and Housing Statute QA, about 10K paired examples.
limits: Authors' argument; statute and exam items only.
agent_relevance: Score analogy retrieval and analogy use as two separate steps.

source: Nguyen et al. (2024) Exploiting LLMs' Reasoning Capability to Infer Implicit Concepts in Legal Information Retrieval
finding: Two LLM query-expansion methods (legal term generation, query reformulation) feed lexical and BERT rankers on COLIEE statute retrieval and beat the competition teams.
numbers: COLIEE 2022 private test F2 0.8449 (P 0.7935, R 0.9005) vs best team HUKB 0.8200: +2.49 points. COLIEE 2023: +0.3 points over CAPTAIN.
limits: Statute retrieval, not precedent retrieval; Japanese civil code; margin small in 2023.
agent_relevance: LLM-extracted implicit concepts help matching, but margins shrink as baselines improve.

source: Zou, Zhang, Weir, Van Durme, Holzenberger (2024) Reframing Tax Law Entailment as Analogical Reasoning
finding: Rewrites SARA statutory reasoning as analogy over pairs of (statute, case): 176 entailment samples become 15,400 analogy samples. GPT models are near chance on the analogy task.
numbers: Zero/few-shot accuracy mostly 49-60%; best gpt-4-0613 zero-shot without think-step-by-step about 68 +/- 3 (table cells garbled in text extraction). Fine-tuned SBERT about 50%; best tuned classifier 50.7% test.
limits: 5 random test sets of 100; small SARA base; exact cell mapping uncertain.
agent_relevance: Analogy judged from raw text by 2023-era models is close to chance. Do not trust an unstructured are-these-alike call.

source: Zou et al. (2024) Reframing Tax Law Entailment as Analogical Reasoning
finding: Retrieve similar solved cases with DPR or BM25 and vote over analogy labels: an old case-based loop on top of newer models. Think-step-by-step often hurt or did nothing.
numbers: Best configuration 57% accuracy (statute+context+hypothesis), above entailment baselines but not statistically significant.
limits: Small test set; the CoT result conflicts with Blair-Stanek et al. 2023 (GPT-3), as noted by Peoples 2025.
agent_relevance: Retrieve, analogise, vote is testable but gains are small. Zero-shot CoT is not a free upgrade for analogy.

source: Gray, Savelka, Oliver, Ashley (2024) Using LLMs to Discover Legal Factors
finding: LLMs induce factor lists (the unit of analogy in HYPO and CATO) from raw opinions. With a human refining the list, factors predict outcomes moderately, below expert-defined factors.
numbers: 173 drug-interdiction cases, 103 with expert annotation. Models gpt-4-turbo and llama-3.1-70b. LLM annotating with expert factors: strong MCC; LLM-refined factor list: weakest.
limits: One domain; fully automated pipeline needs improvement; prompts tuned for proprietary models.
agent_relevance: Likeness features can be discovered by a model, but need review. Auto-made factor sets are the weak link.

source: Peoples (2025) Artificial Intelligence and Legal Analysis: Implications for Legal Education and the Profession
finding: Law-school IRAC exercises, including beginning and skilled analogical problems, on Lexis+ AI, ChatGPT 3.5, Claude, Gemini, Copilot (April-May 2024). Answers were brief, one-sided and falsely confident.
numbers: Total IRAC score out of 56: Claude 50.5 (90%), Copilot 46.4 (83%), GPT-3.5 43.0 (77%), Gemini 41.6 (74%), Lexis+ AI 40.9 (73%).
limits: Rubric graded by one author; few exercises; 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Common-law analogy needs both-sides argument and a committed conclusion; prompts must demand both.

source: Peoples (2025) AI and Legal Analysis
finding: Think-step-by-step improved ChatGPT on only 1 of 3 statutory exercises. This echoes a 2023 tax-law study where 7 of 8 LLMs did not gain, though GPT-4 did.
numbers: ChatGPT 3.5 and Gemini scored 8.5 of 14 on applying the rule.
limits: The 2023 study is cited secondhand; results mixed across tools.
agent_relevance: A generic CoT cue is unreliable for legal analogy; test per step.

source: Ashley (1990) Modeling Legal Argument: Reasoning with Cases and Hypotheticals (HYPO)
finding: HYPO modelled similarity between cases by dimensions, found best analogies, and generated distinctions and counterexamples. Cited in 2510.08710 as the origin of factor-based comparison.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; cited in an opened paper.
agent_relevance: Ground truth for the likeness operator is a symbolic dimension comparison, which the schema can run as code.

source: Aleven & Ashley (1994) CATO factor hierarchy
finding: CATO added a hierarchy linking base factors to abstract legal issues, so a difference can be shown irrelevant to the issue. Used as ground-truth structure in 2510.08710.
numbers: Not read directly.
limits: Secondhand via the 2026 paper.
agent_relevance: The hierarchy is exactly what models fail to integrate.

source: Sunstein (1993) On Analogical Reasoning, Harvard Law Review; Levi (1949) Introduction to Legal Reasoning
finding: Theory side: analogy finds a middle-level principle that explains the cases while staying incompletely theorised. Levi describes reasoning from case to case via a rule that shifts as cases arrive.
numbers: No empirical numbers.
limits: Not opened; recalled from the field, no source read this session.
agent_relevance: Matches the induce, test on each case, revise pattern seen in SILVER.

source: Synthesis across the opened papers (2024-2026)
finding: Models do well on surface overlap and simple typed lookups, and badly at integrating relevance through a hierarchy, abstaining when no analogue exists, and tracking precedent status.
numbers: Task 1 100% vs Task 3 11-34%; abstention 0-86.7%; overruling ID 71-73%.
limits: Different tasks, models and dates; the synthesis is mine.
agent_relevance: The program should hold the factor table, shared-factor set, abstain rule and status check; the model fills one slot at a time.
